front: Why cannot magnetic poles be isolated?
back: Cutting a bar magnet in half gives two smaller magnets, each with a north and south pole. Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist.

front: Properties of magnetic field lines (4 rules)
back: (1) Form continuous closed loops. (2) Tangent gives direction of B. (3) More lines per unit area = stronger B. (4) Never intersect.

front: Far axial field of a bar magnet / solenoid
back: B = (mu_0/4*pi)(2m/r^3). This is the field produced by the equivalent solenoid.

front: Torque on a magnetic dipole in uniform field
back: tau = m x B. In magnitude tau = mB sin(theta), where theta is the angle between m and B.

front: Magnetic potential energy of a dipole
back: U_m = -m . B = -mB cos(theta). Zero at theta = 90, minimum (-mB) at theta = 0 (stable), maximum (+mB) at theta = 180 (unstable).

front: Equatorial field of a bar magnet (r >> l)
Axial field of a bar magnet (r >> l)
back: B_A = (mu_0/4*pi)(2m/r^3). Twice the equatorial magnitude, same direction as m.
E -> B, p -> m, 1/4*pi*epsilon_0 -> mu_0/4*pi.
The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: sum(B . Delta S) = 0. Because monopoles do not exist.

front: Why do magnetic and electric Gauss's laws differ?
back: Electrostatics has sources (charges); magnetism has no monopoles, so field lines form closed loops and net flux is always zero.
M = m_net/V, the net magnetic moment per unit volume. Vector, dimensions L^-1 A, units A m^-1.
B_0 = mu_0*n*I, where n is turns per unit length and I the current.

front: Magnetic field with a material core
back: B = B_0 + B_m, where B_m = mu_0*M is the field contributed by the material.
H = B/mu_0 - M. Same dimensions as M, units A m^-1. Total field: B = mu_0(H + M).
chi = M/H. Dimensionless. Small positive (paramagnetic), small negative (diamagnetic), large positive (ferromagnetic).

front: B in terms of chi and mu_r
back: B = mu_0(1 + chi)H = mu_0*mu_r*H = mu H, where mu = mu_0*mu_r = mu_0(1 + chi).
Diamagnetic: -1 <= chi < 0, 0 <= mu_r < 1. Paramagnetic: 0 < chi < eps, 1 < mu_r < 1 + eps. Ferromagnetic: chi >> 1, mu_r >> 1.
Repelled by a magnet; field lines expelled, field inside reduced (one part in 10^5). Examples: copper, water, bismuth, lead, nitrogen.
Perfect diamagnetism in superconductors (chi = -1, mu_r = 0) - the external field is completely expelled.
Weakly attracted; permanent atomic dipoles align with field; field lines concentrated, field inside enhanced. Examples: aluminium, sodium, oxygen.
Strongly attracted; domains align to form a single 'giant' domain. Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium (mu_r > 1000).
A macroscopic volume (~1 mm, ~10^11 atoms) in a ferromagnet where atomic dipoles spontaneously align with a net magnetisation.
Hard (Alnico, lodestone): retain magnetisation when field removed - permanent magnets. Soft (soft iron): magnetisation disappears.
At high enough temperature a ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet; the domain structure disintegrates with temperature.
H = 2 x 10^3 A/m, B = 1.0 T, M ~ 8 x 10^5 A/m, magnetising current I_M = 794 A for a core of mu_r = 400.
